annotations.text:
DRAWN LIKE A SPORTS MANGA

Everyone here grew up on كابتن ماجد — Captain Majid. This takes the visual LANGUAGE of that 80s football-manga era: halftone screentone, converging speed lines, 3px inked panel borders, leaning impact lettering with a hard shadow behind it. Not its characters or artwork, which belong to their creators — the genre is the part people are actually nostalgic for, and it is yours to use.

Warm newsprint page, kit red, big dramatic sky, flash yellow. Every screen is live — tap the buttons.

The rows read in order: sign up and book · the promise and the occasion · what brings you back.

ROW 1 — GETTING IN

Screen 1 asks the level question in four plain options and then tells you that you can't get it wrong. That is the honest version of onboarding: the rating fixes itself in two games.

Screen 3 is where the guarantee is put in writing, in the exact words we intend to keep — including the part that isn't flattering, in black and yellow at the bottom.

ROW 2 — THE PROMISE, BOTH WAYS

Screens 5 and 6 are two halves of one mechanic. One person gives a shirt up, another takes it, and the refund only exists because the second screen happened.

Screen 5 is the most Tsubasa-era moment in the app — a full-bleed speed-line panel with the ball hanging in the middle of it — and it is pointed at the thing CeleBreak does worst.

Screen 7 names the sides after the night's real fixture, then says plainly that the names change nothing about how teams are picked.

ROW 3 — WHY YOU COME BACK

Screen 10 and screen 11 are deliberately two different screens. Level is how good you are; standing is whether you turn up. Merging them breaks both, so each one says in as many words that the other isn't it.

Screen 12 is the character stats page — huge shirt number ghosted behind, screentone burst. That is the screen people put in the group chat, which is marketing you don't have to buy.

THE ONE RULE

Sunbursts, tilted panels and full-bleed speed lines are reserved for three beats: the goal, the win, and the money coming back.

Everywhere else the page stays flat and calm. Drama that never stops is just noise — the reason the big panels hit is that most screens do not have one.
